scenes.tts: A cut on your finger usually closes in roughly a week or a little longer. Near the tip of an onion root, cells divide, and the root pushes deeper into the soil. In both places, the living thing adds new cells. Why add more cells, instead of letting each cell grow bigger? And how does each new cell get a full set of instructions?
scenes.visual: A skin cut fills with small cells; an onion root tip adds cells; two question boxes appear: bigger? and full set?

scenes.tts: Oxygen, food and wastes all cross the cell membrane. Model a cell as a cube. This is a geometry model, not a measurement. A cube with sides of two units has a surface of twenty-four square units and a volume of eight cubic units. Double the sides to four. The surface grows to ninety-six, the volume to sixty-four. Surface for each unit of volume falls from three to one point five. A bigger cell has less membrane for its inside.
scenes.caption: Oxygen, food and wastes all cross the cell membrane. Model a cell as a cube. This is a geometry model, not a measurement. Surface for each unit of volume falls from 3 to 1.5. A bigger cell has less membrane for its inside.

scenes.tts: The cell cycle is the series of stages from a new cell to its division. Interphase, between divisions, is not a rest. In G one, the cell grows. In S phase, it copies its D N A. In G two, it gets ready to divide. Each copied chromosome is two identical sister chromatids, joined at the centromere.
scenes.caption: The cell cycle is the series of stages from a new cell to its division. Interphase, between divisions, is not a rest. In G1, the cell grows. In S phase, it copies its DNA. In G2, it gets ready to divide. Each copied chromosome is two identical sister chromatids, joined at the centromere.

scenes.narration: The cell cycle is the series of stages from a new cell to its division. Interphase, between divisions, is not a rest. In G1, the cell grows. In S phase, it copies its DNA. In G2, it gets ready to divide. Each copied chromosome is two identical sister chromatids, joined at the centromere.

scenes.tts: Mitosis divides the nucleus. In prophase, chromosomes coil up and the nuclear envelope breaks down. In metaphase, spindle fibers, thin protein fibers, line the chromosomes up across the middle. In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite ends. In telophase, a new nuclear envelope forms around each set.
scenes.visual: One model cell, two chromosomes: envelope fades, bars thicken; spindle fibers line them up; chromatids split and move to the ends; two envelopes form

scenes.tts: Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm. In an animal cell, a ring at the middle pinches the membrane inward, making a furrow, until the cell splits. A plant cell has a stiff wall and cannot pinch. A cell plate grows across the middle and becomes a new wall.
scenes.visual: Left an animal cell pinched by a furrow into two cells; right a plant cell with a cell plate growing across and becoming a wall

scenes.tts: So, why more cells, not bigger ones? One reason is that a bigger cell has less membrane for its inside. And how does each new cell get a full copy? The cell copies its D N A first. Mitosis then shares it out, and the two new cells usually have the same D N A.
